articles.title: As Russia expands attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine prepares to hit Moscow’s oil industry harder in response
articles.body:
Ukraine will intensify strikes on Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanded campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with Reuters on 3 October.
Russia has increased attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, hitting energy and telecommunications infrastructure, roads, railways, and bridges across the Dnipro. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond by targeting the Russian energy infrastructure that helps finance the war.
Russia expands attacks on Kyiv
Russian forces have broadened their strikes on infrastructure in and around Kyiv in recent weeks, with attacks increasingly affecting systems that support civilian life.
Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents indicating that Russian authorities had approved a broader policy for targeting infrastructure, including logistics, roads, schools, and hospitals. He said the goal is to put pressure on residents to leave Kyiv and other major cities.
Russia has also begun targeting bridges across the Dnipro, which connect the eastern and western parts of the capital.
Ukraine targets Russia’s war economy
Ukraine plans to keep striking Russian oil refineries because they generate revenue that supports Moscow’s war effort, Zelenskyy said.
The policy puts Kyiv at odds with US President Donald Trump, who has urged Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, arguing that such strikes contribute to higher global diesel prices.
Zelenskyy said he sees no indication that Moscow is prepared for either peace talks or an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure.
Ukraine prepares for a new wave of air attacks
Ukraine is also preparing for intensified Russian attacks on its energy system over the winter. Ukrainian officials say Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles for a new campaign against electricity and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has also expanded its use of fast jet-powered Geran drones, launching dozens each day since the summer.
Ukrainian F-16s and MiG aircraft are intercepting around 60% of these drones, according to Zelenskyy, but ammunition for their 20 mm cannons is running low. Ukraine is increasing the use of electronic warfare and expects a first shipment of small, inexpensive air defense missiles designed to counter the jet-powered drones later in October.
Ukraine is developing five interceptor drone models to counter Russian Shaheds. Two have already undergone testing, with Zelenskyy putting their current interception rate at around 30%.
Ukraine expands its strike capabilities
Ukraine is also expanding its long-range strike capabilities. It has used its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time, with a range of about 250 kilometers, while work continues on the longer-range FP-9.
At the same time, Kyiv is working with European partners to secure additional funding for its defense needs. Ukraine has found financing to order drones for early 2027 and is working to close a $27 billion gap in this year’s defense budget through its own resources, bilateral assistance, and financing linked to the EU’s €90 billion loan package.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s ability to sustain its defense and expand its strike capabilities will remain central as Russia prepares for another winter campaign.

articles.title: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
articles.body:
Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties, said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities.
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran. While Zelensky has expressed his willingness to try an energy ceasefire, the American president's pleas appear to have gained little traction in Moscow.
In order to help double down on striking Russian energy sites, Ukraine will continue to produce its own long-range ballistic missiles. On Oct. 1, Zelensky announced Ukraine's domestically developed FP-7 ballistic missile was used in combat against Russia for the first time.
Zelensky told Reuters he has already called on the missile's manufacturer, Fire Point, to prepare longer-range missiles.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure," Zelensky said.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI safety leader warns smarter AI could evade safety tests: Report
articles.body:
Halis Sunnetci
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
A former OpenAI safety leader who resigned from his role this week warned Saturday that increasingly capable AI models could recognize when they are being tested and behave differently after deployment.
David Robinson, who spent three and a half years at OpenAI and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches, said in an article for The Atlantic that the industry's approach to safety would lead to further failures unless changes are made.
"Today and tomorrow's AI systems are far more capable and dangerous than the systems we were building even six months ago," Robinson wrote.
His warning comes amid growing concern over increasingly autonomous AI systems, following recent incidents involving agents bypassing safeguards and calls from researchers for companies to slow the development of more powerful systems until safety measures improve.
Robinson called for AI companies to draw more heavily on safety expertise from other high-risk industries and to conduct new research to ensure more capable models behave safely even when they are not being monitored.
"Given today's risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster," he wrote.
Robinson also warned that existing safety evaluations may become less reliable as models grow more capable.
"Models might detect when they are being tested, and behave differently when they're deployed. The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes," he said.
He argued that stronger safety science should be developed before companies create systems significantly more capable than those available today.
"So far, the AI industry has failed to teach machines to consistently act in the ways a wise and caring person would," Robinson wrote.
"Before the organizations building AI can teach a superintelligence to treat humanity well, they'll need to remember how to do it themselves."

articles.title: Portugal investigates US use of Lajes Air Base ahead of Iran war
articles.body:
Burak Bir
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
Portugal’s Public Prosecutor’s Office has opened an inquiry into the legality of US military use of Lajes Air Base ahead of its war against Iran, according to media reports.
The inquiry follows a complaint filed by the Left Bloc in April, which called for an investigation into whether the use of the base violated domestic and international law, broadcaster RTP reported Friday.
The party then asked the Attorney General's Office to investigate whether the use of the base complied with the law, arguing from the outset that it constituted a "gross violation of International Law."
The coordinator of the Left Bloc, Joss Manuel Pureza, stated at the time that "either the Government" was "in agreement with the gross violation of International Law and Portuguese Law," or it lacked the "political backbone" to "remove itself from illegality."
Pureza also questioned the position taken by Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel, who has denied any violation of the agreement between Portugal and the US regarding the military use of Lajes or of International Law.
"I suppose that, moreover, Minister Paulo Rangel himself doesn't believe what he's saying. Because saying that the Lajes Air Base isn't being used for aggressive purposes is pure fabrication. Saying that the Lajes Air Base agreement is being fulfilled is another fabrication."
According to the report, Pureza believes it is necessary to wait for the conclusions of the inquiry, but understands that, "by taking this step," the Public Prosecutor's Office acknowledges that "there is merit" in the complaint filed by the party.

articles.title: Korean pilot Choi Wonkyun wins World Drone Cup at TEKNOFEST Southeast
articles.body:
Efe Ozkan
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
South Korean FPV drone pilot Choi Wonkyun won the World Drone Championship on Saturday after four days of competition at the TEKNOFEST Southeast World Drone Cup.
Choi claimed the title ahead of compatriot Kim Minjae, who finished second, while Bulgaria's Dimo Shterev took third. They were awarded their prizes by T3 Foundation Board of Trustees Chairman and TEKNOFEST Executive Board Chairman Selcuk Bayraktar, Turkish Secretary of Defense Industries Haluk Gorgun and STM General Manager Ozgur Guleryuz.
“I’m really happy to win this competition,” Choi said after the final, thanking his coach and uncle for helping him prepare.
He said preparing for the competition had been difficult but added that he would return to defend his title.
Runner-up Kim said he had opportunities to finish first during the opening rounds but missed his chance.
“It’s obviously totally my fault, and I’m just really disappointed in myself,” he said, adding that he would return stronger next time.
Kim also thanked his parents and sponsors for supporting his participation.
Shterev described his third-place finish as “amazing” and “a bit unexpected” following what he called a disappointing qualifying performance.
“I pushed through the finals. I keep increasing my pace, I keep believing in myself and I keep working on my consistency,” he said.
Shterev also thanked his parents, sponsors and his team, ROC Special in China, for helping him prepare for the race.
A total of 32 drone pilots from around the world competed in the championship, which began Oct. 1, using high-speed first-person-view (FPV) drones they designed and assembled themselves.
The pilots tested their speed, reflexes and control skills on a challenging course that featured moving gates this year.
Türkiye’s prime aviation, space and technology festival TEKNOFEST opened its doors to visitors on Wednesday, this time in the nation’s southeastern province of Sanliurfa.
TEKNOFEST Southeast, a leg of the event held in the southeastern part of the country, brings together tech enthusiasts, young investors and thousands of visitors for various shows, exhibitions and the finals of tech competitions across 14 categories from Wednesday through Oct. 4.

articles.title: In the Kharkiv region, the enemy struck a civilian vehicle with a drone—one person was killed
articles.body:
In the Kharkiv region, the enemy struck a civilian vehicle with a drone—one person was killed
Kyiv • UNN
In the village of Shestakove, a Russian drone struck a civilian vehicle. A 35-year-old woman was killed, and a 39-year-old man was hospitalized.
In Kharkiv region, in the village of Shestakove, a Russian drone struck a civilian vehicle. A woman was killed and another person was injured in the strike. This was reported by Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, according to UNN.
“A hostile drone strike on a civilian vehicle was recorded in the village of Shestakove. As a result of the enemy strike, a 35-year-old woman was killed and a 39-year-old man was injured
The injured man was taken to hospital to receive qualified medical care.
We remind you
On October 3, Russian forces struck a civilian cargo vessel flying the Liberian flag in one of the ports in Odesa region. As a result of the attack, an engine-room sailor was killed, and three other crew members were injured.
